rv.q: Mar a Irene Forn s's ingenious Fefu and Her Friends is such a work, and this revival from director Lileana Blain-Cruz is nothing short of exquisite.
It’s a strong and necessary production.
And a good revival it is — I think; it seems well acted and designed.
It is an evening of glitteringly arranged social chaos, in which high comedy keeps company with many darker undertones.
Four decades after it debuted, Fefu still hits us like a shot between the eyes.

The host, Fefu (Amelia Workman), seems to deliberately push her guests’ boundaries, and has a deeply strange relationship with her unseen husband. Christina (Juliana Canfield) is a newcomer to the group, intimate with Cindy (Jennifer Lim) but not most of the others, and her timidity sometimes crosses the line into whimpering childishness.

Such enjoyably perverse Oscar Wilde-like wit abounds in “Fefu and Her Friends,” but unlike Wilde, Fornes displays no interest in creating a clever plot around her clever remarks – or indeed, much of any plot.

While María Irene Fornés’ Fefu and Her Friends is considered a feminist statement, in performance the play seems not to be very revealing about women or their positions other than the fact that the cast is entirely female.
Fefu and Her Friends is an absorbing and thoughtful, if somewhat enigmatic, work that is distinguished by its unorthodox structure.

There are laughs, and love affairs, and a water fight, and a hunting gun, and much discourse on art. It feels like a Goethe tale that passes the Bechdel test… a thought-provoking triumph for director Lileana Blain-Cruz and the many personalities she and the ensemble have detailed.

cn.t: Fornés's 1977 masterpiece still feels radical in this exquisite revival, with critics praising its innovative environmental staging and ensemble work, though some find the experimental structure more admired than emotionally engaging.
